key_findings.finding: The strongest pediatric human evidence supports an association between nocturnal hypoxia/OSA and more advanced NAFLD. In a biopsy-based adolescent study (PMID 27501738; n=36 NAFLD, 14 lean controls), 69% had OSA/hypoxia; affected participants had more stage-3 fibrosis than those without OSA/hypoxia (36% vs 0%, p=0.03). Higher urinary F2-isoprostanes correlated with apnea/hypoxia index, time with SaO2 <90%, and lower oxygen nadir; hepatic 4-hydroxynonenal staining correlated with hypoxia severity and steatosis. This directly supports nocturnal hypoxemia as a plausible oxidative-stress-linked promoter of pediatric NASH/fibrosis, but the study is observational and small.

Pediatric aggregate evidence is directionally positive but largely cross-sectional. A meta-analysis of 9 cross-sectional studies including 1,133 children/adolescents (PMID 32881371) found OSA associated with higher ALT, AST, and NAFLD fibrosis stage, but not histologic inflammation grade; associations with ALT/AST persisted in studies matched for age, sex, and BMI.
